standard.title: Voice as a literary device
standard.description: compare and evaluate how 'voice' as a literary device is used in different types of texts, such as poetry, novels and film, to evoke emotional responses
standard.prior_knowledge: Students create and edit literary texts including hybrids, experimenting with structures, features and devices for purpose (AC9E9LE06). They have not yet compared and evaluated how voice as a literary device evokes emotional responses across different text types.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students compare and evaluate how 'voice' as a literary device is used in different types of texts to evoke emotional responses.

nodes.label: Understanding voice as a literary device
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify how voice operates as a literary device in a text, explaining how the author constructs voice and what it contributes to the text.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify how voice is constructed in a provided text and explain what it contributes to the text's meaning or effect.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how voice is constructed as a literary device across at least two different text types (poetry, prose, film), explaining how voice choices shape meaning and tone in each.
wider: Examine how protest voice in poems or songs constructs a sense of collective identity and emotional urgency
Analyse how First Nations Australian authors use voice as a literary device to assert identity and challenge dominant narratives
Examine how unreliable narrators in novels construct a voice that evokes both sympathy and unease
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to compare and evaluate voice across text types — a move that collapses without the conceptual precision about what 'voice as a literary device' means. Students who retain colloquial uses of 'voice' cannot make meaningful cross-text-type comparisons.

response_modes.reason: Voice is a conceptually slippery term — students need explicit scaffolding to distinguish 'voice' as a literary device (constructed textual persona) from colloquial uses of 'voice'; the reasoning move from textual choices to constructed voice needs support.

success_criteria: Identifies how voice is constructed in a text through specific literary choices
Explains what the constructed voice contributes to the text's meaning or tone

nodes.label: Comparing and evaluating voice across text types
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare and evaluate how voice as a literary device evokes different emotional responses across poetry, novels and film.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare how voice is used in at least two different text types and evaluate how each evokes a different emotional response.
nodes.typical_width: Compare and evaluate how voice as a literary device evokes emotional responses across a range of text types — poetry, prose and film — making supported judgements about the effectiveness of each.
wider: Compare the voice of protest across a range of poems, songs and speeches and evaluate how different voices evoke different emotional responses from different audiences
Evaluate how voice in a film creates a different emotional response than the same story told through prose, analysing what the medium change does to the voice
Examine how First Nations Australian authors use voice across text types to evoke emotional responses that challenge or illuminate dominant perspectives

response_modes.reason: Voice functions very differently across poetry, prose and film — students who only analyse voice in one text type may assume it works the same way everywhere; cross-text-type comparison is the essential context variation here.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Comparative voice analysis across poetry, fiction and film offers rich material — protest voices, First Nations Australian voices and unreliable narrators all provide sustained comparative work.
success_criteria: Compares how voice as a literary device operates in at least two different text types
Evaluates how each use of voice evokes a different emotional response, with textual evidence
